2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate risk / concern: PNSB non-response is low (188/5,507 municipalities in 2000 and 133/5,564 in 2008; Table 2, PDF p. 6), but excluding boundary-splitting municipalities, missing covariates, and kernel-matching common support reduces the two-group project sample from 1,175 municipalities (Table 1, PDF p. 4) to an unbalanced panel of 1,899 observations across 1,008 municipalities in Table 4 cols. 1-3 and 955 complete municipal pairs in the bootstrapped difference test in col. 4 (~18.7% attrition from the 1,175 total; PDF p. 8). Pre-2000 municipal splits also restrict the 1990-2000 pre-trend check to 556 municipalities (865 observations; Table 5 col. 6, PDF p. 9), though a Nijman-Verbeek selection indicator (st1) finds no significant structural difference (PDF pp. 9-10).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk / concern: Municipality fixed effects (DiD) combined with multinomial probit kernel matching (Heckman et al., 1997, 1998; Lechner, 2001, 2002), an urban access placebo regression (Table 5 col. 2, PDF p. 9), and a 1990-2000 pre-trend check (Table 5 col. 6, PDF pp. 9-10) remove time-invariant heterogeneity and municipality-wide trends. However, two ROBINS-I confounding issues remain: (1) unobserved time-varying differences in external donor/state financial and technical support bundled with WUA umbrella models in Northeast Brazil (CENTRAL, KfW-funded SISAR, PROSAR, CAERN subsidies; PDF p. 3) alongside inability to separate municipal water/sanitation spending from health expenditure (Table 3 note, PDF p. 7); and (2) conditioning the preferred propensity-score specification (Table 10 cols. 7-9; Appendix A.4, PDF pp. 19-21) on concurrent/post-baseline changes during 2000-2008 and 2000-2010 (Change to regional main, Change to local main, Delta Pop dens, Delta Admin).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate quality: Section 2 (PDF pp. 3-4) accurately situates municipal decentralization, CESB concessions, the 2007 national sanitation law's social-control councils (conselhos gestores), rural development councils, and WUA concession/umbrella arrangements (CENTRAL, SISAR, PROSAR), informed by 36 retrospective semi-structured telephone interviews in 2013-2014 (Section 4(b), PDF pp. 6-7; Appendix A.1, PDF p. 15). Empirically, however, institutional governance is operationalized via a coarse municipality-level binary indicator from PNSB (2000 and 2008) that merges dual-provider municipalities (Main + loc + assoc) into the WUA treatment category (Note 9, PDF p. 13; Table 7, PDF p. 16), lacks district-level coverage shares or contract rules, and uses a generic 2008 municipal participation indicator in Table 6 without knowing its institutional form or whether it preceded the water project (PDF pp. 11-12).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate risk (Moderate for exposure classification, Low for outcome measurement): Provider governance and piped-water outcomes come from independent national IBGE instruments (PNSB 2000/2008 and Demographic Census 2000/2010). However, exposure measurement exhibits moderate misclassification risk because municipalities with both new local-government and WUA rural systems (256 municipalities in 2008; Table 2, PDF p. 6) are pooled into +assoc (Note 9, PDF p. 13), exact project start dates within 2000-2008 are unknown, and projects started in 2009-2010 fall between the 2008 PNSB exposure wave and the 2010 Census outcome wave (PDF p. 4). Outcome measurement via national census enumeration is standardized and objective across groups.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Good for physical household connection rates, limited for service quality: Rural piped-water access on premises from the general network is measured consistently across all Brazilian municipalities using the 2000 and 2010 IBGE Demographic Censuses (PDF pp. 3-4). However, as the author explicitly notes (PDF p. 4), municipality-level rural connection rates do not capture water quality/potability, supply continuity/hours, system disrepair, or intra-community equity, cannot isolate treated rural districts from untreated rural districts within the same municipality, and are observed in 2010 (two years after the 2008 PNSB provider wave).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: No information (no pre-analysis plan or protocol): No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan exists to verify whether the propensity-score covariate set, matching bandwidth/specification, or the six accountability channel interactions in Table 6 (PDF p. 11) were pre-specified. Transparency is aided by extensive robustness tables (Tables 4-5, Appendix Tables 10-12), though one sensitivity check mentioned in Note 9 (treating Main + loc + assoc as a separate unweighted category; PDF p. 13) is not tabulated.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk / concern: The study draws on the national universe of Brazilian municipalities in the 2000/2010 Censuses and 2000/2008 PNSB, comparing municipalities with new WUA (n = 583) versus new local-government (n = 592) rural water systems (and n = 3,717 no-change municipalities in Table 12). Excluding municipalities that split boundaries between 2000 and 2008 (PDF p. 5) and restricting to complete covariates and matching support drops ~14.2% of project municipalities in Table 4 (1,008 of 1,175 municipalities), though a Nijman-Verbeek test for pre-2000 boundary splits shows no significant selection bias (Table 5 col. 7, PDF pp. 9-10).

domain_ratings.justification: The study combines municipality fixed effects (DiD) with multinomial probit propensity-score kernel matching (reducing standardized bias below 20% on baseline covariates; Figure 1, PDF p. 8; Table 11, PDF pp. 20-21) and validates parallel trends via a 1990-2000 pre-trend test (Table 5 col. 6, PDF pp. 9-10) and an urban piped-water placebo test (Table 5 col. 2, PDF p. 9). Nevertheless, ROBINS-I rates D1 as Serious for two reasons: (1) unmeasured time-varying project financing and external technical assistance co-varying with WUA expansion, particularly in Northeast Brazil where donor/state umbrella organizations (CENTRAL, KfW-funded SISAR, PROSAR, CAERN subsidies; PDF p. 3) supplied dedicated funding and technical blueprints while municipal water/sanitation expenditure cannot be separated from health expenditure (Table 3 note, PDF p. 7); and (2) inclusion of concurrent/post-baseline variables measured over 2000-2008 and 2000-2010 (Change to regional main, Change to local main, Delta Pop dens, Delta Admin) in the preferred propensity-score specification (Table 10 cols. 7-9, PDF pp. 19-20; Appendix A.4, PDF p. 21), conditioning matching weights on post-intervention changes (partially mitigated by similar unweighted DiD estimates in Table 12).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 (PDF pp. 3-4), Section 3 (PDF p. 5), Table 3 (PDF p. 7), Section 5 & Table 5 (PDF pp. 8-10), Table 10 & Appendix A.4-A.5 (PDF pp. 19-23)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: The sampling frame covers all Brazilian municipalities in IBGE's 2000/2010 Censuses and 2000/2008 PNSB. Primary matched DiD regressions restrict to municipalities that introduced either a WUA or local-government rural system during 2000-2008 (with comparisons against 3,717 no-change municipalities also shown in Appendix Table 12, PDF p. 22) and exclude municipalities whose borders split between 2000 and 2008 (Section 4(a), PDF p. 5). Covariate missingness and matching common-support restrictions narrow the project sample from 1,175 municipalities (Table 1, PDF p. 4) to 1,008 municipalities in Table 4 (PDF p. 8). While a Nijman-Verbeek test on pre-2000 municipal splits finds no structural selection bias (Table 5 col. 7, PDF pp. 9-10), post-2000 split exclusions and conditioning on project initiation introduce Moderate risk.
domain_ratings.where_found: Table 1 (PDF p. 4), Section 4(a) & Table 2 (PDF pp. 5-6), Table 4 (PDF p. 8), Section 5 & Table 5 col. 7 (PDF pp. 9-10), Appendix Table 12 (PDF p. 22)

domain_ratings.justification: Intervention status is derived from IBGE's National Basic Sanitation Survey (PNSB) in 2000 and 2008, an independent survey recorded prior to the 2010 Census outcome wave. However, three classification limitations yield Moderate risk: (1) municipalities where both a local government and a WUA operated additional rural systems (256 Main + loc + assoc municipalities in 2008; Table 2, PDF p. 6) are grouped into the +assoc treatment indicator (Note 9, PDF p. 13; Table 7, PDF p. 16), contaminating pure governance comparisons (Note 9 states separating them unweighted does not change results, but does not tabulate the estimate); (2) exact implementation dates within 2000-2008 and projects initiated in 2009-2010 (between the 2008 PNSB and 2010 Census) are unobserved (PDF p. 4); and (3) treatment is a binary municipality-level indicator that does not capture the share of rural districts covered or variation in actual community participation (PDF p. 4).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 & Table 1 (PDF p. 4), Section 4(a) & Table 2 (PDF pp. 5-6), Note 9 (PDF p. 13), Appendix Table 7 (PDF p. 16)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: In observational policy terms, co-interventions were not fully balanced across governance arms: in Northeast Brazil, WUA systems were frequently supported by state/donor umbrella organizations (CENTRAL, SISAR/KfW, PROSAR, CAERN mainline connection programs; Section 2, PDF p. 3) providing external technical assistance and organizational blueprints alongside user management, and concurrent rural water initiatives (One Million Cisterns, Water for All, Programa Agua Doce; PDF p. 4) operated in semi-arid areas (though targeting cisterns/desalination rather than piped networks). Subgroup interactions showing significant positive WUA effects in Southern Brazil where donor umbrella programs were rare (+assoc * south = 0.0773**; Table 5 col. 3, PDF p. 9) and robustness to main-supplier switches (Table 5 col. 4; Table 12 cols. 2-6) bound this risk at Moderate rather than Serious.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2 (PDF pp. 3-4), Section 5 & Table 5 cols. 3-4 (PDF pp. 9-10), Appendix Table 12 (PDF pp. 22-23)

domain_ratings.justification: PNSB item/unit missingness is modest (188/5,507 municipalities in 2000 and 133/5,564 in 2008; Table 2, PDF p. 6), but cumulative exclusions from boundary splits, missing probit/regression covariates, and kernel-matching support reduce the two-arm sample from 1,175 municipalities (2,350 potential observations; Table 1, PDF p. 4) to an unbalanced panel of 1,899 observations across 1,008 municipalities in Table 4 cols. 1-3 and 955 complete municipality pairs in the bootstrapped difference test in col. 4 (~18.7% attrition; PDF p. 8). In the 1990-2000 common-trend test, municipal splits reduce the sample to 556 municipalities / 865 observations (Table 5 cols. 5-6, PDF pp. 9-10); although the Nijman-Verbeek test (st1) supports ignorable attrition from pre-2000 splits, no formal missing-data sensitivity analysis or imputation addresses covariate/panel missingness in the 2000-2010 sample.
domain_ratings.where_found: Table 1 (PDF p. 4), Table 2 (PDF p. 6), Table 4 (PDF p. 8), Section 5 & Table 5 cols. 5-7 (PDF pp. 9-10), Appendix Table 12 (PDF p. 22)

domain_ratings.justification: The outcome—share of a municipality's rural population/households with piped water on premises from the general network—is measured from the 2000 and 2010 IBGE Demographic Censuses using standardized national household enumeration protocols across all municipalities, completely independent of the PNSB provider classification and blind to the study's comparative governance hypothesis. Differential measurement error in the defined connection outcome across +assoc and +loc municipalities is therefore unlikely (Low ROBINS-I outcome-measurement bias, even though physical connection rates do not capture water quality or service continuity as noted on PDF p. 4).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-analysis plan, registered protocol, or pre-specified econometric specification is reported. While the paper transparently presents unweighted and kernel-weighted DiD specifications, three multinomial probit models, municipal and state-level clustering, urban and pre-trend placebos, and regional/supplier interactions (Tables 4-5; Appendix Tables 10-12), one sensitivity check cited in Note 9 (analyzing Main + loc + assoc as a separate unweighted category; PDF p. 13) is not tabulated and the six political-accountability interaction regressions in Table 6 (PDF pp. 11-12) cannot be verified against a pre-specified plan. Per ROBINS-I guidance when no protocol/pre-analysis plan exists, D7 is rated No information.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 5 & Table 4-5 (PDF pp. 7-10), Section 6 & Table 6 (PDF pp. 10-12), Note 9 (PDF p. 13), Appendix A.4-A.5 (PDF pp. 21-23)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Barde (2017) conducts a comparative longitudinal quasi-experimental evaluation of Brazilian municipalities between 2000 and 2010, combining municipality fixed-effects difference-in-differences (DiD) with multinomial probit propensity-score kernel matching (informed by 36 auxiliary semi-structured telephone interviews conducted in 2013-2014) to test whether rural small-scale piped water supply systems implemented and managed by water user associations (+assoc) expand rural household tap connections more than systems implemented and managed by local governments (+loc). Methodological strengths are substantial relative to prior cross-sectional rural water studies: national IBGE Demographic Census (2000, 2010) and PNSB sanitation survey (2000, 2008) coverage, standardized census outcome measurement (Low risk in D6), covariate balancing below 20% standardized bias, a null urban piped-water placebo check, an insignificant 1990-2000 pre-trend test on non-splitting municipalities, and a Nijman-Verbeek split-sample check. Under ROBINS-I, however, overall risk of bias is Serious, driven by Domain 1 (Confounding): (1) unobserved time-varying project capital investment and external donor/state technical and financial support bundled with WUA umbrella programs in Northeast Brazil (CENTRAL, KfW-financed SISAR, PROSAR, CAERN subsidies) cannot be separated from community governance, and municipal water/sanitation expenditure is combined with health spending; and (2) the preferred propensity-score specification (Table 10 cols. 7-9) conditions on concurrent/post-baseline changes during 2000-2008 and 2000-2010 (changes in main supplier, population density, and administrative spending). Moderate concerns also arise in D2-D5 from pooling dual-provider (Main + loc + assoc) municipalities into the +assoc treatment arm, asynchronous exposure (2000-2008) and outcome (2000-2010) windows, ~14-19% panel/matching attrition, and bundled regional co-interventions, while D7 is rated No information due to the absence of a pre-analysis plan.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative longitudinal municipal panel study using difference-in-differences (DiD) combined with multinomial probit propensity-score kernel matching (2000-2010 Census and 2000-2008 PNSB), informed by 36 auxiliary retrospective semi-structured telephone interviews for propensity-score covariate selection.
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research design and identification strategy in Abstract (PDF p. 1), Section 1 (PDF pp. 2-3), and Section 3 (PDF p. 5); institutional context, outcome scope, and exposure/outcome timing in Section 2 & Table 1 (PDF pp. 3-4); PNSB/Census panel construction, boundary-split exclusions, and 36 auxiliary telephone interviews in Section 4 & Table 2-3 (PDF pp. 5-7) and Appendix A.1 (PDF pp. 15-16); main weighted DiD, urban placebo, regional/supplier interactions, 1990-2000 pre-trend check, and Nijman-Verbeek attrition check in Section 5 & Tables 4-5 (PDF pp. 7-10); accountability heterogeneity in Section 6 & Table 6 (PDF pp. 10-12); intervention coding and sensitivity notes in Notes 5-16 (PDF p. 13) and Appendix A.2-A.5, Tables 7-12 (PDF pp. 16-23).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the exact design-matched instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study's primary empirical design is a non-randomized comparative evaluation of competing governance interventions (water user association vs. local government rural water supply systems) using longitudinal panel difference-in-differences combined with multinomial propensity-score kernel matching (Section 3, PDF p. 5). Although Section 4(b) (PDF pp. 6-7) and Appendix A.1 (PDF p. 15) report 36 semi-structured telephone interviews conducted in 2013-2014, these interviews play an auxiliary covariate-selection role for the propensity-score specification (explicitly described by the author on PDF p. 12 as "anecdotal evidence provided by sector experts in the interviews, which informed this study") rather than constituting a co-equal mixed-methods primary study, making ROBINS-I more appropriate and informative than MMAT.
